newsitem.title: USA: Clinton and Dole get set for Sunday debate.
newsitem.headline: Clinton and Dole get set for Sunday debate.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole both played down their abilities on Friday as they rehearsed intensively for Sunday's first presidential debate.

"I'm badly out of shape on this, but I'm trying to get better," a smiling, relaxed Clinton told reporters as he emerged from a lakeside hotel serving as his pre-debate headquarters to enjoy the glorious autumn weather at the Chautauqua Institution, a quiet Victorian-era resort in western New York state.

Turning to former Senate Democratic leader George Mitchell, who is impersonating Dole in dress rehearsals for the Hartford, Connecticut, debate on Sunday night, Clinton said: "Tell the truth, George. You beat me like a drum. You kicked me all over the place last night."
Buttressing the president's effort to lower expectations, Mitchell said he probably debated Dole more than anyone else when they were in the Senate together "and I know just how effective he is."
"Senator Dole is a highly skilled debater, and I think he's going to be tough in this debate coming up on Sunday. But the president, I think, will do all right," he said.

Dole has been playing down his expectations for weeks, and on Friday he said of the debate, which he and his aides hope will pump new life into his floundering campaign: "Ready or not, it's going to happen. It will be very, very interesting."
"I think it's always important to challenge the president. The president always has somewhat of an upper hand," a nervous-sounding Dole told reporters.

"He is the president. He can do things. He can say things," he said as he took a brief break from dress rehearsals conducted in the ballroom of the south Florida ocean-front condominium complex where he has an apartment.
The Dole campaign began airing a new advertisement blasting Clinton as a tax-and-spend liberal who tries to present himself as a centrist.
A Reuters tracking poll showed Clinton widening his lead over Dole to 14.3 percentage points. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot's support dropped to 4.4 percent, its lowest level yet.

Perot, who performed well in the 1992 debates, has been excluded this year because of his low poll ratings. The Federal Communications Commission slammed another door in his face on Friday, rejecting the Texas billionaire's request that the big television networks be forced to sell him more prime time for campaign commercials.
The FCC decided unanimously that the networks acted legally in refusing to sell Perot extra prime-time slots for his half-hour campaign "infomercials."
Later a U.S. appeals court killed his last hope of blocking his exclusion. The three appellate judges upheld the key parts of a lower-court ruling that rejected Perot's arguments.
With polls showing that almost 80 percent of voters think Clinton will win the Nov. 5 election, Dole badly needs to land some heavy blows on Sunday to turn the race around.

The Reuters poll showed voters were giving Clinton fairly good marks for his handling of the Israeli-Palestinian crisis. Nine percent called the president's performance "excellent," 33 percent said it was "good," 29 percent said it was "fair," and 14 percent rated it "poor."
Dole has been taking the debate extremely seriously, cutting back on campaign appearances to practice in mock encounters in which Tennessee Sen. Fred Thompson plays the part of Clinton.
Dole and his handlers publicly stress they are up against a masterly speaker in Clinton, while privately they pray their man can establish himself in 90 minutes as a viable alternative.
"Everybody knows how good Clinton is on his feet, but I think Senator Dole's honesty, knowledge and integrity will show through," Thompson said.
